newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus prepares to end its cap on interest rates. [CORRECTED 12:51 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Cyprus prepares to end its cap on interest rates. [CORRECTED 12:51 GMT]

text.p: Cyprus is pushing forward with radical reforms to its monetary system, including scrapping a ceiling on interest rates early next year.
But the liberalisation, in preparation for negotiations to join the European Union, may come as a rude shock to Cypriots used to easy loans at a maximum rate of 8.5 percent.

"The political decision for full deregulation has been taken, but we will have to make sure there are safeguards to avoid it having a disturbing effect on the economy," Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou said earlier this week.
Commercial bankers say a target date of January 1 has been set for scrapping the 50-year-old law which sets the interest rate ceiling.
"(Legislation) will be tabled to the House of Representatives for approval before the end of the year," Christodoulou told Reuters.
The ceiling, imposed by the former British colonial administration of the island, was aimed at curbing usury, but its effect has been to prevent the use of interest rates in credit policy.
Cyprus is now under increasing pressure to align its legislation with the European Union before it starts accession talks, scheduled for early 1998.
"There is the psychological aspect, and the need to accept the changes by the public and groups, which we do not ignore," said Christodoulou.
A primary concern of opponents of deregulation is whether Cypriots, heavily in debt already for home or car purchases, may wake up one morning to find their mortgage rates have soared.
Sixty percent of adult Greek Cypriots have a mortgage, according to some analysts, and the small print says banks can modify the rate without notice.
(Corrects to clarify that it is 60 percent of adult Greek Cypriots who are in debt, not 60 percent of all Cypriots).
Personal loans accounted for 55 percent of all loans issued in the first five months of 1996, according to official statistics.
They show personal loans reached 1.07 million pounds ($2.29 million) at the end of May, a 29 percent increase from May 1995.

"The government said it will ensure that rates are not changed for persons with old loans once deregulation takes place, but I do not see that happening," said Stavros Evagorou, an economic researcher at the Akel communist party, staunch opponents of deregulation and the second largest party in the House of Representatives, which has to approve the legislation.
An economist at a major Cypriot bank agreed. "In theory, yes, there is no guarantee rates will remain the same. But my feeling is that the authorities will do their best not to upset the market.
"My guess is that they will try to administer the change by removing the ceiling and imposing new guidelines to define rates," he said.
"They might introduce constraints on housing loans which are very sensitive so that they can't fluctuate beyond a given band."

Cooperatives, which issue the bulk of housing loans, are opposed to deregulation. They have little to gain if the rates go up since they already lend at their maximum capacity - but plenty to lose if rates go down, to banks offering a wider range of facilities to their clients.
The finance ministry and the central bank have tried to ease borrowers' concerns by arguing that Cypriots will have the option of turning to foreign banks for their loans if local rates are too high.
Deregulation goes hand in hand with easing restrictions on the movement of foreign capital, they say.
Question marks remain over the status of offshore banks on the island, which, according to one central bank scenario, would be able to grant loans in foreign currency.

"We will fight this if this happens," said the banking source. "Offshore banks pay 4.25 percent corporate tax compared to 25 percent paid by local banks, and it will be unfair competition if they are allowed to enter the local market."
Earlier this year the central bank took the first step towards reform by creating a money market through regular treasury bill auctions under repurchase agreements.
